Here's a model that gets every example it trained on right. A hundred percent. Show it examples it has never seen, and it gets eighty-four. Which of those is the model? Most of the machine learning round comes back to that gap. Fifteen questions in this round. Every figure you'll see is a real model, fitted in Python. The last three are quick. First, where the gap comes from.

Question one. Explain the bias-variance trade-off. Twenty noisy points from a sine wave. A straight line is too rigid to follow the curve. That's bias: error from assumptions that are too simple. A degree-nine polynomial bends through the points, noise and all. That's variance: error from fitting this one sample too closely. Degree three sits between them. Make the model more flexible, and training error only falls. Validation error falls, bottoms out at degree three, and climbs again. The best model is at the bottom of that curve, not at its end. Question two. How do you detect and fix overfitting? Look for the gap: good on training data, poor on held-out data. At degree nine, training error is point oh six, and validation error is five point seven. To fix it: more data, a simpler model, regularization, early stopping, and cross-validation, so the estimate is honest. One of those fixes gets a question of its own.
